cases.abstract: VoxPoser turns language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to satisfy affordances and constraints jointly rather than sequence predefined actions. Pretrained language models generate programs that query visual perception and compose three-dimensional voxel maps; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from updated observations without additional training. Across five tabletop robot tasks, success averages 88% without disturbances and 70% with disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for a language-model-plus-primitives baseline. This comparison supports spatial composition as an alternative to primitive sequencing for these tasks, including disturbed execution. Category-level gains over that baseline and learned costmaps on 13 simulated tasks support transfer to unseen instructions and attributes, but task-level improvements are uneven. For contact-intensive simulated door, window, and fridge tasks, zero-shot trajectories alone are insufficient; using them as exploration priors concentrates action sampling near relevant interactions. Dynamics learning then takes under three minutes of online interaction, whereas exploration without priors exceeds a twelve-hour limit, supporting the trajectories' additional role in guiding learning for contact-intensive tasks. The approach depends on manually supplied prompt examples and perception, and its implementation plans end-effector rather than whole-arm trajectories.
cases.notes: Revision decision: connect joint spatial objectives to the primitive-sequencing comparison, not claim that this comparison isolates a causal mechanism. Sections 3.2-3.4 and Tables 1-3 support trajectory synthesis, held-out generalization, and exploration-guided dynamics learning; Table 4 preserves uneven task-level evidence. Contact learning remains simulation-only. The zero-shot regime uses pretrained models and manual prompt examples; planar pushing still uses a predefined primitive. Table 3 leaves dispersion undefined, so none is inferred. Perception, dynamics, and end-effector-only planning bound the claims.

cases.abstract: Training loss at a single parameter vector can conceal differences in test performance among minima. Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) instead minimizes worst-case loss in a weight neighborhood with weight regularization, favoring solutions whose nearby parameters also have low loss. A PAC-Bayesian bound motivates this objective when Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss and the parameter norm is at least one; it does not certify the practical approximation. SAM perturbs weights along the gradient and updates using the perturbed-weight gradient, dropping second-order terms and requiring two backpropagations. On CIFAR-10/100, gains over baselines allowed up to twice as many epochs support benefits beyond longer pointwise training: AutoAugment WideResNet reduces CIFAR-10 error from 2.2% to 1.6%. ImageNet training and pretrained EfficientNet finetuning also improve. Clean-test accuracy improves under random label corruption, but SAM trails MentorMix; bootstrapping narrows the gap without eliminating it at the highest noise rate. Complementary analyses find lower Hessian curvature and show that separate neighborhood maximizations on smaller subsets improve SAM generalization and make m-sharpness more predictive of generalization gaps in the studied settings. These diagnostics support neighborhood-based optimization without establishing curvature as the isolated cause, and an augmented SVHN configuration worsens.
cases.notes: Revision decision: use the longer-training CIFAR comparator to test value beyond extending pointwise optimization, while retaining theory-to-implementation separation. Section 2 and Theorem 2 supply the neighborhood objective and assumptions; Tables 1-3 support classification and finetuning, not an unconditional guarantee or shared training budget. Table 4 retains MentorMix and bootstrapping qualifications; Table 5 retains the SVHN reversal. Section 4 contributes subset-wise maximization and m-sharpness diagnostics. Curvature is corroborating geometry, not an experimentally isolated explanation for the accuracy gains.
